ARG.story:
Between 1976 and 1983 Argentina was ruled by a military junta, a government of the heads of the armed forces. Security forces secretly detained people they saw as opponents, and many were never seen again; they became known as the disappeared. Children kidnapped with their parents or born to mothers in detention were taken and registered as the biological children of military families or supporters of the regime. Many did not know they were adopted. The practice crossed borders under Operation Condor, an agreement among South American military governments to hunt each other's opponents. In one case, a pregnant 19-year-old Argentine detained in Buenos Aires in 1976 was moved secretly to Montevideo, and her baby was given to a Uruguayan police officer's family, who raised her under another identity for 23 years.

In 1977 the children's grandmothers formed the Grandmothers of Plaza de Mayo to search for them. Their work led to the creation of a National Bank of Genetic Data, which allowed DNA tests to match children with their families. About 500 children are estimated to have been taken. The Grandmothers had found 97 by 2008 and announced the 140th in July 2025. In 2012 a federal court in Buenos Aires found that the junta had run a systematic plan to take these children. It sentenced the former dictator Jorge Videla to 50 years and the last dictator, Reynaldo Bignone, to 15 years.

The Italian priest Nicola Corradi was accused at a school for deaf children in Verona in 2009, and he went on working at the same order's school for deaf children in Luján de Cuyo, in Mendoza province. He was arrested there in 2016, and in 2019 a Mendoza court sentenced him to 42 years and another priest to 45 for abusing children at the school between 2004 and 2016.

Most of the children taken under the junta have still not been identified, and those who are found learn their true identity as adults.

BEL.story:
In 1992 Belgium released Marc Dutroux early from a 13.5-year sentence for rape, against the objections of a prosecutor and a psychiatrist. In 1995 and 1996 he kidnapped six girls aged 8 to 19. His mother wrote to the authorities in 1995 that he was holding two girls, but police took 14 months to arrest him. Police missed voices heard in his cellar and did not review his videotapes, and rivalry between two police forces slowed the search. In October 1996 hundreds of thousands of people marched in Brussels in protest. A parliamentary inquiry criticised the police investigation, and Belgium later reorganised its police forces. In 2004 Dutroux was sentenced to life. Witnesses also told investigators of an abuse network involving prominent people, but prosecutors dismissed the statements and the claims remain unproven.

The Catholic Church set up its own commission in 2000. It upheld 32 of 33 formal complaints, but 31 were past the statute of limitations, the legal deadline for bringing a case, and only one reached court. In April 2010 the Bishop of Bruges, Roger Vangheluwe, resigned after admitting he had abused his nephew from 1973 to 1986. A second church-backed commission then received 475 complaints in six months, and its report recorded 13 suicides linked to abuse by clergy. In June 2010 police raided church buildings, including the archbishop's palace in Mechelen, and seized the commission's files and 450 internal dossiers.

Eric Dejaeger, a Belgian missionary in the Canadian Arctic, fled to Belgium in 1995 and lived in homes of his order for 16 years despite an international warrant. Returned to Canada in 2011, he was sentenced in 2015 for 32 offences against Inuit children.

After the church cases, abuse in Flemish youth institutions and boarding schools from 1930 to 1990 came to light, and in 2014 the Flemish Parliament formally apologised to the victims.

Much of the abuse in Belgian church institutions was reported after the legal deadlines had passed. Victims of abuse in Flemish institutions are still coming forward, and the commission set up in 2014 to hear them received 121 reports in 2024.

BRA.story:
In 2000 Brazil made it a crime, punishable by 4 to 10 years in prison, to subject a child or adolescent to prostitution. Foreign men continued to travel to the coast of the northeast for sex with children, and in 2006 the Federal Police said this happened most often in Fortaleza, Recife, Salvador and Natal. In its 2025 report on trafficking, the US State Department said that taxi drivers and staff of hotels, bars and nightclubs in coastal tourist towns help arrange the sale of children for sex. It cited a study suggesting that up to 16 percent of girls aged 14 to 17 in one northeastern city area were likely victims. It also said a 2016 case against an elected official in Paraná was unresolved.

Children are also sold along the country's main roads. For about 19 years the Federal Highway Police and the charity Childhood Brasil have mapped roadside places such as truck stops, bars and motels where children are at risk. Their survey for 2021 and 2022 assessed more than 9,700 places and rated 640 critical. An earlier survey found that 38 percent of victims came from elsewhere and may have been trafficked.

Brazil also sent children abroad for adoption, 5,456 of them between 2003 and 2022. In 2021 a Dutch government inquiry found serious violations in adoptions from several countries, Brazil among them, between 1967 and 1998, and the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption.

Brazil has the largest Catholic population in the world, but no national inquiry into abuse in the Church or other institutions has been found. In 2010 former altar boys in Arapiraca complained about three priests, and a secretly filmed video was shown on television. In 2011 a court convicted the three of abusing altar boys and sentenced them to between 16 and 21 years, but they were not jailed while they appealed.

Without a national inquiry, the extent of abuse in Brazil's churches, schools and care homes is not known. Children are still sold for sex along the main roads and in tourist towns, and Brazil reported no investigations of officials involved.

CHE.story:
From 1926 to 1973 the Swiss foundation Pro Juventute ran a programme it called the Charity for the Children of the Country Road, which took around 600 Yenish children from their families and placed them in children's homes or with foster families. The Yenish are one of Switzerland's travelling peoples. Federal and cantonal authorities, the national and regional governments, shared staff with Pro Juventute and helped pay for the programme. In February 2025 the Swiss government accepted a legal opinion that the persecution of the Yenish and Sinti was a crime against humanity.

The same authorities also detained people without any court order. An independent expert commission reported in 2019 that more than 60,000 people had been held in about 650 institutions, mainly between 1930 and 1981, and that many were abused physically, psychologically and sexually. Among them were the Verdingkinder, children placed with farmers as unpaid labourers. The government had apologised in 2010, and a 2016 law gave each victim of these measures a payment of CHF 25,000.

Switzerland also received children for adoption from abroad, including 1,111 from South Korea between 1968 and 1997 and others from Sri Lanka, India and Tibet. Swiss authorities realised early that the children were often wrongly described as orphans and that some adoptions were linked to organised child trafficking, yet they decided cases on incomplete or false documents. After parliament commissioned a study in 2018, the Federal Council, Switzerland's government, acknowledged these failures in 2020 and 2023, and at the end of 2024 it recommended banning intercountry adoption altogether.

In 2023 historians at the University of Zurich, working for the Catholic bishops and religious orders, documented 921 victims of abuse in the Swiss Catholic Church since the 1950s; 74 percent of the documents concerned abuse of minors. They described their count as the tip of the iceberg.

Switzerland has examined and apologised for removals and detentions carried out by its own authorities, and has paid victims of compulsory measures. The researchers' count of victims in the Catholic Church is a minimum, and the full number is not known.

DEU.story:
From 1967 the youth authorities of West Berlin, the city's child welfare service, followed the advice of the sexologist Helmut Kentler and placed homeless boys and other children with men known to be paedophiles as foster fathers. University of Hildesheim reports in 2020 and 2024 found the Berlin authorities responsible and found that a network of academics, welfare officials and educators across West Germany tolerated or supported this until after 2000. Kentler died in 2008 without being prosecuted.

One member of that network was Gerold Becker, headmaster of the Odenwaldschule, a private boarding school in Heppenheim. Former pupils reported abuse in 1998 and a newspaper wrote about it in 1999, but a promised review did not take place, and prosecutors dropped the case because the statute of limitations, the legal deadline for bringing a case, had passed. In 2010 a report commissioned by the school named Becker and a music teacher as the main abusers, and later counts put the victims at 132 pupils or more. Becker died that year without facing a court.

After abuse at another school, the Canisius-Kolleg, became public in January 2010, the federal government set up a Round Table on child sexual abuse and an Independent Commissioner. In 2013 the Bundestag, the federal parliament, extended the deadline for civil claims from 3 to 30 years. A 2022 report for the Archdiocese of Munich and Freising counted at least 497 victims since 1945 and found misconduct by Joseph Ratzinger, archbishop from 1977 to 1982 and later Pope Benedict XVI, in four cases.

At a campsite in Lügde two men abused 32 children from 1998 to 2018, and a youth office had placed a foster daughter with one of them. Police received two tips in 2016, and 155 pieces of evidence went missing from a police office. A state parliamentary inquiry said the men could have been stopped two years earlier. Both were convicted in 2019.

The main figures in the Kentler and Odenwaldschule cases died without trial. The Lügde abuse continued until 2018, after the 2010 reforms, while police and a youth office had information about the offenders.

ETH.story:
In the 2000s the number of Ethiopian children adopted abroad grew quickly. The number sent each year rose from 262 in 2002 to more than 3,887 in 2008, and between 2003 and 2022 a total of 33,303 children left the country this way. The United States alone issued 15,166 visas to adopted Ethiopian children between 1994 and 2014. Families in Canada found that children had been given papers as orphans when their parents were alive. In 2011 the US State Department found that one agency, Better Futures Adoption Services, was involved in child trafficking, and the agency lost its licence to work in Ethiopia.

Ireland suspended adoptions from Ethiopia in 2007, Australia in 2009 and Denmark in 2016. Ethiopia suspended foreign adoptions in November 2017, and in January 2018 its parliament banned adoption by foreigners. It cited abuse and neglect of children abroad after a US couple were convicted in 2013 over the death of an adopted Ethiopian girl.

During the war in Tigray, which began in 2020, forces on both sides raped women and girls. A UN-appointed commission of human rights experts reported in 2022 that Ethiopian and Eritrean forces had committed widespread sexual violence in Tigray, and that Tigrayan forces had raped women and girls as young as 11 in Amhara villages in 2021. In February 2021 the BBC reported that 200 girls under 18 had registered at health centres in Mekelle as survivors of rape. In 2024 the UN verified sexual violence against 73 children in Ethiopia, and attributed 38 of these cases to the national army.

Ethiopian girls are also taken abroad. The US State Department's 2025 report on trafficking says traffickers exploit them as domestic servants and for sex in Djibouti and Sudan, sometimes using drugs to control them, and that begging rings exploit women and children in Saudi Arabia. It said reports of officials taking part continued.

Foreign adoption from Ethiopia has been closed since 2018. The national army was responsible for more than half of the sexual violence against children that the UN verified in Ethiopia in 2024.

FRA.story:
Between 1963 and 1982 the French state took about 2,000 children who had been made wards of the state on Réunion, a French island in the Indian Ocean, and sent them to rural departments of mainland France that were losing population, such as Creuse. Some were adopted, and others stayed in children's homes or were made to work on farms. In 2014 the National Assembly, the lower house of parliament, passed a resolution saying the state had failed in its moral responsibility towards these children. No compensation has been planned.

France also took in children from abroad, including 11,165 from South Korea between 1968 and 2008. In March 2024 a government assessment acknowledged that the authorities had long known of "illicit practices of a systemic nature" in intercountry adoption and had been late to act.

In 2018 the Catholic bishops set up an independent commission chaired by Jean-Marc Sauvé. Its 2021 report used a population survey to estimate that about 216,000 people had been abused as minors by priests and members of religious orders since 1950, or about 330,000 if lay people working for the Church were included.

In 2004 the FBI, the US federal police, traced downloads of abuse images to the surgeon Joël Le Scouarnec, and in 2005 a French court gave him a four-month suspended sentence. Prosecutors did not tell the medical authorities, a warning to the health ministry in 2007 led to no action, and in 2008 a hospital hired him knowing of the conviction. He went on abusing patients until 2014. In 2025 he admitted abusing 299 victims, many of them under anaesthesia, and was sentenced to 20 years, the maximum.

In April 2025 a parliamentary inquiry estimated that about 15,000 children in the care of the departmental child welfare services are victims of prostitution. Teenagers in care are often housed in hotels with little supervision.

France has estimated the scale of abuse in the Church through a national survey and has given victims more time to bring a case. By the inquiry's estimate, about 15,000 children in the state's own care are being sold for sex now.

GHA.story:
Among the Ewe people of Ghana, some traditional shrines practise trokosi. A shrine takes a girl, usually a young virgin, to atone for a wrong a relative is said to have committed. She serves the priest without pay, and in most shrines sexual service to the priest is treated as part of her duty, which defenders of the practice deny. In 1998 Ghana amended its Criminal Code to make ritual or customary servitude a crime, with a minimum sentence of three years. The practice continued, and no prosecutions are recorded.

Children are also sold into work. On Lake Volta, traffickers put children as young as four to work in fishing and control them with violence and little food. In 2023 International Justice Mission, a charity, surveyed 1,286 children in three fishing districts and estimated that 37.7 percent were likely to have been trafficked. The US State Department said in 2025 that girls in the fishing trade are at risk of sexual exploitation, and that observers reported forced child labour on the lake had decreased. In cocoa farming, a study funded by the US government estimated that 1.56 million children in Ghana and Côte d'Ivoire worked in cocoa in 2018 and 2019, almost all in hazardous work. Chocolate companies had promised in 2001 and 2010 to cut the worst forms of child labour by 70 percent by 2020. The study found that child labour in cocoa had increased since 2008 while production rose.

Some Ghanaian boys were taken further away. In 2019 police in Kaduna, in northern Nigeria, raided a building presented as an Islamic school and freed more than 300 boys and men, many of them in chains. Some had been brought from Ghana, Burkina Faso and Mali, and local media reported that captives had been sexually abused.

No representative survey of online sexual exploitation of children has been carried out in West and Central Africa, so its extent in Ghana is not known. Children are still put to work on Lake Volta and on cocoa farms, and trokosi continued after it was made a crime.

ISR.story:
In Israel's first years, from 1948 to 1954, babies of newly arrived immigrant families were taken to hospitals and the parents were later told that they had died. More than 1,000 families, most of them from Yemen and others from the Balkans, North Africa and the Middle East, say their children disappeared this way, and many believe the children were given away for adoption. Three government inquiries since the 1960s concluded that most of the children died of disease and were buried without their parents being told. In 2021 the government expressed regret and approved compensation of NIS 162 million.

In March 2008 the Adass Israel School, an ultra-Orthodox school in Melbourne, paid for its headmistress, Malka Leifer, to fly to Israel before the police were told of allegations that she had abused pupils. Australia issued a warrant in 2014 for 74 offences. Her lawyers in Israel sought more than 70 hearings and appeals, and in 2019 she was found to have faked mental illness. The deputy health minister, Yaakov Litzman, had pressured ministry staff to change psychiatric evaluations so that she would appear unfit for extradition, the legal process of sending a suspect to another country for trial. Leifer was extradited in 2021 and convicted in Melbourne in 2023 of 18 charges including rape. Litzman admitted breach of trust in a plea deal, resigned from the Knesset, Israel's parliament, and received eight months' probation.

In June 2024 a UN Commission of Inquiry found that Israeli security forces had subjected Palestinians to sexual violence during arrests and in detention, that men and boys were targeted in particular ways, and that this amounted to gender persecution as a crime against humanity. It also found that sexual violence was committed in the attacks of 7 October 2023, when 36 children were among 252 people taken hostage.

The fate of many of the children who disappeared in the early years is still unknown to their families. Leifer was convicted 15 years after she left Australia, and the minister who obstructed her extradition received probation.

JPN.story:
Johnny Kitagawa founded Johnny & Associates, which became Japan's dominant agency for boy bands, which trained boys to become pop singers. A weekly magazine first reported on his abuse of boys in 1965. In 1999 the magazine Shūkan Bunshun published a series of reports, and Kitagawa sued it for defamation, a claim of false and damaging reporting. The courts upheld the reporting on sexual abuse in 2003 and 2004. Japanese newspapers and television barely covered the rulings; journalists said this was because the agency controlled which of its stars appeared on their programmes. Kitagawa died in 2019 without being charged.

A BBC documentary in March 2023 and a former trainee's public statement in April led the company to set up an outside investigation. Its report in August 2023 found that Kitagawa had abused boys and young men from the early 1970s to the mid-2010s. The company admitted the abuse, split off its talent business, and set up a committee of three former judges to handle compensation. By August 2026 it had decided to compensate 585 people.

In June 2023 Japan reformed its Penal Code, the main criminal law. It raised the age of consent from 13 to 16 and extended the time limit for prosecuting rape from 10 to 15 years.

Other institutions have been counted only in part. In 2020 the Catholic bishops published a survey of all 16 dioceses that found 16 cases of abuse of minors from the 1950s to the 2010s. Most victims had taken 10 to 30 years to report, and eight of the accused had been transferred. In 2021 the newspaper Yomiuri Shimbun found that at least 47 staff in children's homes had committed indecent acts against 69 children in their care over five years.

In Japan most abuse became known only when victims spoke decades later or foreign media reported it. Children are still sold for sex through "JK businesses", which sell dates with high-school girls; the police counted 91 such businesses at the end of 2024, and the US State Department says many have links to organised crime.

MMR.story:
In 2017 Myanmar's armed forces, the Tatmadaw, carried out what they called "clearance operations" against the Rohingya, a minority people in Rakhine State. A UN inquiry, the Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Myanmar, found in 2018 that hundreds of Rohingya women and girls were raped during these operations, and that 80 percent of the corroborated cases were gang rapes. In 2019 it reported that sexual violence was a hallmark of the army's operations in Rakhine, Kachin and Shan States. It also found that in 2012 Rohingya men and boys, some as young as twelve, had been subjected to sexual violence while held at Buthidaung prison.

In 2019 Human Rights Watch documented women and girls from these areas, many of them displaced, who had been sold for US$3,000 to $13,000 to families in China as brides. They were locked up and raped so that they would become pregnant. One girl was trafficked at 16 by her sister-in-law. Human Rights Watch said police in both countries gave traffickers little reason to fear arrest. In 2025 the US State Department said displaced women and girls in Kachin and Shan remain at risk of forced marriage and forced childbearing in China.

The war has continued. In 2024 the UN verified the abduction of 85 children, most of them to be used as fighters, 41 by the armed forces and their militias and 33 by the Kachin Independence Army, an ethnic armed group.

Children in Buddhist monasteries are another group with little protection. Up to 300,000 children may live in monasteries, and few records are kept. In 2018 four girls aged 10 to 14, who stayed at a monastery in Pathein so they could go to school, said its administrator monk had raped them repeatedly. He disappeared when their parents went to the police. Reporters found that police usually defer to the religious authorities in cases against monks.

The armed forces that the UN inquiry found responsible for widespread rape are still fighting, and children in the conflict areas are still being abducted and trafficked to China.

MOZ.story:
After a peace treaty ended Mozambique's war in 1992, the United Nations sent a peacekeeping mission, ONUMOZ, to oversee the settlement. A UN study of children in armed conflict, led by Graça Machel and published in 1996, found that ONUMOZ soldiers had recruited girls aged 12 to 18 into prostitution. The same study found that in six of twelve countries it examined, the arrival of peacekeeping troops was followed by a rapid rise in child prostitution. Peacekeepers can be tried only by their own countries, and the UN can do no more than send them home.

Since 2017 armed groups linked to the Islamic State have fought in Cabo Delgado, in the north. In 2024 the UN verified that they had abducted 468 children, 371 boys and 97 girls, most of them to use as fighters, and that five girls were subjected to sexual violence. Government forces were also named. Of the 12 girls the UN verified as victims of sexual violence in 2023, five were attributed to the national army and three to a police unit, the Rapid Intervention Unit.

In the south, according to the US State Department's 2025 report on trafficking, traffickers exploit girls at rest stops, bars and restaurants along the highway from Maputo to South Africa and around mines. Girls as young as 11 who work as nannies are at risk when their jobs end.

Bishop Carlos Ximenes Belo, a Nobel Peace Prize winner, left Timor-Leste in 2002 and worked in Maputo from 2004. In 2019 the Vatican received allegations that he had abused boys in Timor-Leste, and in 2020 it limited his ministry and barred him from contact with minors, but it did not make this public until a magazine reported the case in 2022.

Children in Cabo Delgado are still being abducted by armed groups and abused by some of the forces sent to fight them. In the south, girls are exploited along the main trade route to South Africa.

NPL.story:
In March 2007 the British newspaper the Daily Telegraph reported that babies in Nepal were being bought for intercountry adoption, with bribes paid and birth families deceived. The next month Nepal's new minister halted all adoptions abroad. About 440 pending cases were processed from November 2007. The United States later stopped adopting Nepali children declared abandoned, because their documents could not be relied on. Between 2003 and 2022, 1,991 children were sent abroad for adoption.

Children are also placed in children's homes for money. In 2021 and 2022 Nepal's National Child Rights Council counted 417 registered homes holding 10,905 children, and UNICEF estimates that about 85 percent of children in them have a living parent or guardian. Agents take money from poor rural families with promises of schooling and are paid commissions by the homes. In one case documented by charities, a child was admitted with a forged certificate of a parent's death. Researchers say the homes use the children to attract donations from abroad. A 2018 law requires local governments to appoint child welfare officers, but only about 200 of 753 had done so.

Girls and women are also taken to India, across a 1,850 km open border. Estimates collected by researchers put the number at 5,000 to 10,000 a year. Traffickers recruit them with false offers of jobs or marriage, and now also through online romance scams, and sell them to brothels in Kolkata, Mumbai and other cities. Traffickers give underage girls false documents stating they are adults. Inside Nepal, a 2024 study cited by the US State Department found that most workers in the adult entertainment sector were trafficking victims, nearly half of them children. Nepali courts convicted 406 traffickers in the year covered by the 2025 report, which also raised serious concerns about officials taking part.

No representative survey of online sexual exploitation of children has been carried out in South Asia, so its extent in Nepal is unknown. Most children in Nepal's homes have a parent, and the officials meant to check on them have mostly not been appointed.

ROU.story:
In 1966, under Nicolae Ceaușescu, Romania banned abortion by Decree 770, and many of the children born in the following years were abandoned in state institutions. There they were neglected, sedated, and physically and sexually abused; abuse was reported to be common at the children's psychiatric hospital in Siret. After Ceaușescu fell in 1989, television showed about 100,000 children in Romanian orphanages, and foreign families began adopting them in large numbers. Private agencies charged €7,500 to €25,000 per child, and the system soon became corrupt. The United States alone issued 5,285 visas to children adopted from Romania between 1994 and 2008.

Romania tried several times to stop the trade. It halted adoptions in 1991 and outlawed selling babies, imposed a temporary ban in 2001 after a government commission found that middlemen and officials had taken the money, and in June 2004, under pressure from the European Union, banned foreign adoption except by grandparents. In 2006 there were no intercountry adoptions.

Girls from Romania continued to be sent abroad by other means. From 2009 one criminal group used the "loverboy" method, in which a man pretends to be in love with a vulnerable girl. The group exploited girls in prostitution in Romania until they turned 18 and then moved them to Britain, Ireland and Germany. Romanian and British investigators working together arrested 21 members in 2020. In its 2025 report the US State Department said most identified victims of trafficking from Romania are women and girls exploited at home or in Western Europe. It also said children in state institutions, particularly girls in homes for people with disabilities, are at risk of sex trafficking. Romanian courts convicted 161 traffickers in 2024.

Romania also hosted 21,188 web addresses with abuse material removed by the Internet Watch Foundation, a British charity, in 2025, 7 percent of the total.

Foreign adoption from Romania has been closed since 2004. Children still live in state institutions, where girls are at risk from traffickers and some staff are alleged to have been complicit or negligent.

SRB.story:
Serbia kept children and adults with mental disabilities in large state institutions. In 2007 Mental Disability Rights International, a US-based advocacy group, published the results of a four-year investigation covering more than 17,000 people in these institutions. It found children and adults tied to beds or kept in cribs for years, dirty conditions, contagious disease and no outside oversight, and it described the treatment as "tantamount to torture". It also warned of a risk of sexual exploitation. At the institution in Vršac men and women lived in mixed wards, and staff said they made no effort to find out whether sex was consensual. In 2006 the director of one institution had refused to let the investigators see a locked area and asked them to leave, and Serbian officials dismissed the findings as propaganda.

Serbia was also a transit route for trafficking. After NATO troops and UN administrators arrived in neighbouring Kosovo in 1999, women and girls were brought there for forced prostitution, mainly from Moldova, Romania, Ukraine and Russia by way of Serbia. Amnesty International reported in 2004 that the international presence produced 80 percent of the traffickers' income at the time.

No official inquiry into these institutions is recorded, so it is not known whether conditions for the children in them changed after 2007.

TCD.story:
In October 2007 members of a French charity, Zoé's Ark, were detained in Abéché as they tried to fly 103 children to host families in France. The charity said the children were orphans from Darfur, a region of neighbouring Sudan, but the authorities found that most were from Chad and were not orphans. In December 2007 a Chadian court convicted six French members of attempting to kidnap the children and sentenced them to eight years of forced labour. They were transferred to France, and in March 2008 Chad's president, Idriss Déby, pardoned them.

Chad's own army has also been named by the UN. In 2022 the UN verified rape and other sexual violence against three girls by the Chadian National Army in Lac Province, near Lake Chad, where armed groups are active. It also attributed to the Chadian army four of 35 verified cases of sexual violence against girls aged 12 to 17 in Sudan. In the Lake Chad region, the UN verified the abduction of 191 children in Lac Province and in Diffa.

No representative survey of online sexual exploitation of children has been carried out in West and Central Africa, and no national inquiry is recorded, so the extent of abuse of children in Chad is not known.
